When I was writing my Africa Day post in May, it reminded me just how many of you have been cheering on Cajou Espoir since it launched in 2004. For over two decades, you have followed our journey to bring opportunity and dignity to rural Togo. In that moment, I felt it was time to give you a proper update. Some F5ers may have nudged me on that point too. 😉  

To help with that update, I sat down with Gavin Daly, an author and former journalist who recently joined our F5 team. Gavin’s objectivity, curiosity, and fresh eyes are exactly what this update—and you—deserve.   

Before you dive in, it’s important to understand that while Cajou Espoir is my main way of giving back, it is structured as a business, specifically a B2B social enterprise that’s committed to reinvesting in rural Togolese communities. This structure is a conscious choice. The long-term goal is for this job creator to outlive me.  

Here’s Gavin’s take on our conversation about the challenges and joys of creating a truly sustainable and scalable social enterprise. To everyone who has cheered us on or asked how the business is doing over the years, thank you. This update on our continuing evolution is for you.

Our analysis of 250+ active July vacancies reveals a massive, aggressive pivot across the European life sciences sector.

- Simultaneous Scaling: US biotechs have abandoned staggered entries. They are now building commercial structures in 5+ European countries all at once to beat the 2030 patent cliff.

- The Tech "Plumbers" Boom: The hype around AI is hitting reality. Hiring is flooding with demands for the backbone: Cloud, DevOps, and Data Governance engineers.

content:
5 Things to Check Before Accepting a Job Offer... 👀

Receiving a job offer is exciting, but before you say "yes", take a few minutes to check the details.

1. Salary & Overtime
Make sure you understand your pay, overtime rates, and when you'll be paid.

2. Working Hours & Shift Pattern
Confirm your weekly hours, shift schedule, and whether weekend or night work is required.

3. Location & Travel
Is the workplace easy to get to? If you're relocating, ask what support is available.

4. Contract & Benefits
Check your holiday entitlement, pension, bonuses, and any additional company benefits.

5. Career Progression
Will you have opportunities to learn new skills and progress within the company?

Taking a few extra minutes to review your offer can help you make the right decision for your future.

content:
“I’ve got years of experience… why am I still getting rejected?”

This is a question I hear from experienced professionals just as often as I hear it from international students.

Meet Sujeet Tanga ( https://lnkd.in/gdWeSWds )

An experienced #SupplyChain & #Logistics professional who had been trying to secure the right opportunity in the UK for almost two years.

Like many professionals, he did everything he thought he should.

Applied online.

Updated his CV.

Kept searching.

Kept hoping.

Yet the outcome remained the same…

Rejection after rejection.

When Sujeet reached out to us at Job Bridge Recruitment Ltd, we didn’t tell him to apply for another 500 jobs.

We rebuilt the entire strategy.

✔ Targeted employers that genuinely hire

✔ Tailored CVs and applications

✔ LinkedIn optimisation and networking

✔ Interview coaching and preparation

✔ A roadmap focused on quality, not quantity

Three months later, Sujeet secured a role as a Senior Buyer / Purchasing Lead with a £36K+ salary at an excellent UK company.

A fantastic outcome and a well-deserved opportunity.

Sujeet was on a dependent visa, which meant #sponsorship wasn’t a barrier for him.

However, many talented international professionals and graduates don’t have that advantage.

That’s why I always remind people:

Whatever visa you’re on, time matters.

Every month spent following the wrong strategy is a month you don’t get back.

The UK job market hasn’t stopped hiring.

It has simply become more competitive and more strategic.

Whether you’re an experienced professional or a recent graduate, success rarely comes from sending more applications.

It comes from sending the right applications to the right employers with the right positioning.

Congratulations, Sujeet! 👏

Wishing you every success in your new role.

📩 If you’ve been applying for months—or even years—without seeing the results you deserve, perhaps it’s time to rethink the strategy rather than your potential. My inbox is always open.

content:
Recruiters hiring for remote digital roles are increasingly ignoring the dates on a CV to focus on the links in a portfolio.

We have observed a recurring pattern where highly qualified African professionals miss out on global opportunities not because they lack the skill but because they lack the proof. In a digital economy, five years of experience is a claim, while a public project is evidence.

When a founder or a project manager is hiring a Virtual Assistant or a Digital Marketer from across the continent, they are often looking for one thing: Can this person do the work right now?

A resume might say you understand project management. A shared Trello board or a case study of a past project shows how you actually think and organize. This shift from credentials to competence is why many self-taught individuals are outcompeting degree holders for remote roles.

One practical way to adapt is to stop only updating your resume and start building a Proof of Work folder. This could be a collection of published articles, a screen recording of a technical process you mastered, or a folder of design assets.

At Elimika Africa, we focus on helping learners move beyond theory into creating these tangible assets. Our training is designed to ensure that by the time you finish, you have more than a certificate; you have a portfolio that speaks for you.

For those who consistently demonstrate high-quality work, there are often opportunities for additional visibility through our partnership with Outsourced African Talent when roles align with their skills.

What is the most important item in your digital portfolio right now?

"If you try to hire 50 people in Latin America and you're an unknown, it's going to be difficult."

That's the reality Brian Samson lays out on this episode of The Nearshore Cafe — and it's a lesson a lot of companies learn the hard way.

His advice for scaling a LATAM team the right way:
→ Start with 1-2 exceptional, senior hires — people with leadership potential
→ Let them navigate the market and stress-test cultural fit
→ Confirm you've got the right country before you scale

Sound familiar? It's the same approach a New York company would take expanding into Atlanta. You don't hire 50 people in month one — you prove the model first.

The difference in LATAM is trust. It's a high-trust society, and referrals carry serious weight. Reputation opens doors that cold outreach simply can't.

content:
A common observation across our community is the gap between finishing a course and landing a role. Many professionals spend months collecting digital badges and PDF certificates, yet their portfolios remain empty.

The reality of the digital economy is that a certificate proves you were present for a lecture, but a portfolio proves you can solve a specific business problem.

In distributed teams and remote work environments, employers care less about where you studied and more about what you have built. If you are learning social media management, a recruiter wants to see a content calendar you designed. If you are a virtual assistant, they want to see the Notion workspace you built to organize a project. If you are a data analyst, they want to see the dashboard you created from a messy dataset.

We often encourage learners at Elimika Africa to prioritize the project over the paper. Documenting your process and showing your work is what builds trust with a potential client or employer.

Through our partnership with Outsourced African Talent, we have seen that visibility often follows proof of work. Standout learners who can demonstrate their skills through tangible projects are the ones who capture the attention of partners when opportunities align.

What project are you currently building to showcase your skills?

Nigeria’s Biggest Entry-Level Problem Isn’t a Lack of Talent. It’s the Experience Paradox.

One of the biggest frustrations facing young professionals in Nigeria is surprisingly simple:

You need experience to get an entry-level job.

But how do you gain experience if no one is willing to hire you in the first place?

It’s a contradiction thousands of graduates face every year.

The conversation has become so common that it’s being discussed across Nigerian communities, where many graduates describe “entry-level” roles asking for two to five years of experience. Similar frustrations appear in global job discussions as well, showing that this paradox extends beyond Nigeria.  

The challenge isn’t that young Nigerians lack ambition.

It’s that too many never get the opportunity to prove themselves.

At RISE, we believe credibility shouldn’t only come from years of experience. People should also have meaningful ways to demonstrate reliability, consistency, and potential.

Many employers hiring for remote roles across Africa are quietly moving away from prioritizing the graduation year on a CV.

The focus has shifted toward the portfolio of evidence.

Recruiters are increasingly looking for specific links that prove competence. This might be a GitHub repository for a developer, a Figma file for a designer, a published strategy for a digital marketer, or a Google Drive folder containing documented project reports for a virtual assistant.

However, there is a nuance we often observe in the digital space. It is not just about having a portfolio. It is about the organization of that proof. A disorganized link to a folder of unnamed files is often viewed as a sign of poor communication or a lack of attention to detail.

The candidates who stand out are those who present a case study. They clearly explain the problem they faced, the process they followed, and the result they achieved. This structure tells a hiring manager how a candidate thinks, not just what tools they can use.

At Elimika Africa, we prioritize this transition from learning to doing. We encourage our community to focus on building tangible projects that reflect workplace realities rather than just collecting certificates.

Standout learners who build high-quality portfolios may also gain additional visibility through the Elimika Africa and Outsourced African Talent partnership when specific opportunities align.

What does your current portfolio say about your professional process?

⚠️ Professional Alert for Executives

A colleague recently faced an aggressive recruitment‑style scheme:
a “recruiter” promising senior leadership roles, followed by a push toward an external “CV expert” using free email accounts and very intensive, persistent follow‑up to pressure him into paid services.

No verified company.
No job IDs.
No hiring managers.
Just a funnel.

If you receive similar outreach, verify everything:

• corporate email domain
• official website
• registered business details
• real requisitions
• legitimate recruiter affiliation

Stay vigilant. Protect your data and your time.
Not every “executive opportunity” is real.

Free cheese is only found in a mousetrap.

content:
The Psychology of Celebrating Our People: Why Every Work Anniversary Matters


As HR professionals, we often focus on performance, engagement, retention, and results. But there is another factor that deserves just as much attention: the emotional meaning of time.

When someone celebrates a work anniversary, we are not simply recognizing another year on a calendar. We are recognizing the moments behind it: the challenges overcome, the skills developed, the relationships built, and the contribution made to something larger than oneself.

From a psychological perspective, recognition reinforces a sense of belonging, purpose, and value. It tells people: Your time here has mattered. Your work has been seen. Your contribution has made a difference.

Celebrating our talent is not about creating a culture of constant praise. It is about creating moments of meaningful recognition—because people are more than their job titles or performance metrics. They are part of the story we are building together.

As HR professionals, we have the opportunity to make recognition intentional, authentic, and human.

Because when we celebrate someone’s journey, we are not only honoring their past—we are strengthening their connection to the future they are helping us build.

People remember how a company made them feel. Let’s make sure they feel that their time, effort, and contribution truly mattered.

content:
In Ruli, Rwanda, miners haul 30-70 kg bags of tungsten out of tunnels for 10 to 50 cents a bag. 
Their entire work history lives as tick marks in a paper booklet.

Across Africa's informal economy, workers build skills and prove themselves for years. Then a job ends, and the record of it vanishes. 
That missing history shapes access to finance, insurance, and the next job.

Fixa is fixing this. 

They started as a labour contracting platform in Rwanda, supplying workers into construction. But every worker onboarded, every shift completed, every payroll run was quietly creating something that barely exists across the continent: verified employment data. 

So far, more than 20,000 digital employment identities, over 1 million shifts, and US$6 million in wages processed. Over 95% of their workers accessed earned wages for the first time in their lives.

What made us confident?
Plenty of platforms try to sell financial services into the informal economy before they've earned trust or built data. 
Fixa works the opposite way. Solve a real operational problem for employers first, build trusted employment records as a by-product, then use those records to unlock better services for workers.

We think every worker deserves to own a verified record of the work they've done. 

If that becomes part of Africa's labour market infrastructure, Fixa will have helped build it.

📊 Employer Market News

For years, many professionals living north of the Harbour Bridge have accepted the daily commute into central Auckland as part of working life.
But we are seeing a continued shift in the employment landscape — with more businesses and professionals embracing the opportunity to live local, work local.

The northern Auckland employment market is becoming increasingly diverse, with growth and opportunity across key commercial areas:

🔹 Albany & North Harbour — continuing to attract professional services, technology, corporate operations, and expanding business hubs.

🔹 Wairau Valley — a stronghold for trades, automotive, logistics, manufacturing, and service-based businesses.

🔹 Takapuna & Milford — established commercial centres supporting professional, medical, finance, and service industries.

🔹 Silverdale & the Hibiscus Coast — a rapidly developing area with continued residential and commercial growth creating new employment opportunities.

What does this mean for employers?

Local talent is becoming increasingly valuable — but attracting the right people requires more than simply advertising a vacancy.

Today’s candidates are considering:
✔ Commute and lifestyle impact
✔ Workplace culture and values
✔ Career development opportunities
✔ Stability and reputation of the employer

For businesses north of Auckland, your location can be a genuine competitive advantage — but only if your recruitment strategy communicates the value of working locally.

The takeaway:
The northern employment market is growing, but the best candidates will still be selective. Employers who understand their market and position themselves well will be the ones who attract and retain great people.

✈️ Workforce Reality | Growth Watch
Sometimes the biggest hiring story starts with a runway—not a job posting.
When people hear "economic development," they often think of ribbon cuttings and new buildings.
I think of future careers.
This week, one of the biggest workforce stories in Hernando County isn't a company announcing hundreds of new jobs—it's the continued transformation of the Brooksville–Tampa Bay Regional Airport & Technology Center.
A $13.6 million federal investment is helping prepare approximately 600 acres for future industrial and aviation-related development.
That may not sound exciting...
But here's why it matters.
Today's infrastructure projects become tomorrow's hiring announcements.
☕ Coffee Break

Why This Matters
The airport and technology center already support more than 150 companies, and county leaders are positioning the area to attract additional:
Aviation and aerospace companies
Advanced manufacturers
Logistics and distribution operations
Industrial and technology businesses
While no official job numbers have been announced for this latest infrastructure project, previous airport expansions have included new hangars and additional full-time positions—and this investment is designed to create the conditions for more growth.
Here's the Workforce Opportunity
As our region grows, we shouldn't wait until employers start hiring.
We should be asking:
Do we have enough skilled workers?
Are local students aware of these career paths?
Are training providers preparing people for these industries?
Are employers connected to the workforce resources already available?
Those conversations should happen now—not after a company announces it's hiring.
A Message to Employers
Many businesses don't realize there are no-cost workforce resources available to help with recruiting, job postings, hiring events, candidate screening, and connections to training opportunities.
The sooner workforce planning begins, the easier hiring becomes.
A Message to Job Seekers
Pay attention to where investment is happening.
The best career opportunities often start long before the "Now Hiring" signs go up.
The people who prepare early are usually the first to benefit.
Reality Check
Economic development isn't just about attracting businesses.
It's about making sure local people are ready to grow with them.
I'll be watching this project closely because I believe it's one of the most important long-term workforce developments in Hernando County.

If you could bring one new industry to Hernando County, what would it be—and why?

📊 Public Sector Finance & Procurement Recruitment: The Market in 2026

The demand for skilled finance and procurement professionals across London, the South East and the Home Counties remains incredibly strong, despite continued budget pressures.

Several trends are shaping the market right now:

🔹 Public procurement accounts for approximately £385 billion of annual spend, with increasing scrutiny around value for money, supplier performance and social value outcomes. 
🔹 Organisations continue to face shortages of specialist talent, particularly across procurement, commercial management, finance business partnering, transformation, digital and programme delivery functions. 
🔹 Vacancy pressures remain high across many public sector organisations, driving continued reliance on interim and agency resource while permanent hiring remains challenging in key disciplines. 
🔹 The implementation of the Procurement Act has increased demand for professionals with expertise in governance, compliance, contract management and strategic sourcing. 

What's particularly interesting is the shift we're seeing from"cost control" to "skills control". Employers are becoming less focused on simply filling vacancies and more focused on securing the specialist capabilities needed to deliver transformation, efficiency savings and better public services. 

The most successful organisations I work with are:

✅ Moving faster through recruitment processes
✅ Investing in succession planning
✅ Offering flexible working arrangements
✅ Clearly communicating career development opportunities and organisational purpose.

In a competitive market, candidates have choices.

As a recruiter specialising in public sector finance and procurement appointments across London, the South East and Home Counties, I'm finding that organisations able to articulate their long-term vision and employee value proposition are consistently attracting the strongest talent.

I'd be interested to hear from hiring managers and candidates:

👉 Is the biggest challenge currently attracting talent, retaining talent, or securing approval to hire?

Could your next great employee already be out there...waiting for someone to give them a chance?

The Government's Youth Guarantee is designed to do exactly that.

Through the Jobs Guarantee, eligible employers can offer a fully funded six-month placement to young people who have experienced long-term unemployment, with Government covering wages (25 hours per week), employer National Insurance and minimum pension contributions, alongside funding to support onboarding and equipment. 

The programme starts with pilot areas across:

📍Birmingham & Solihull
📍East Midlands
📍Greater Manchester
📍Hertfordshire & Essex
📍Central & East Scotland
📍South West & South East Wales

As the programme expands nationally, it's worth asking a simple question:

Could your organisation offer someone their first meaningful opportunity?

Many employers talk about skills shortages. Sometimes the answer isn't finding experienced people. It's creating opportunities for people with potential.

If you're interested in getting involved, it's well worth exploring the programme and contacting your regional delivery partner. I've added the GOV.UK link in the comments.

Today, that work has a home. HBIC, the Home Office Bureau of Innovation & Competitiveness, is the policy, strategy, and research institute of HYDE. Some of our publications will remain freely available because stronger institutions ultimately benefit everyone. At the same time, HBIC is available to governments, businesses, investors, nonprofits, and institutions seeking independent research, strategic planning, policy analysis, institutional design, and long-term economic thinking.

We believe that thoughtful ideas deserve the same level of craftsmanship as the products and companies built from them.

content:
Reposting this because the upcoming changes to unfair dismissal protection will make one thing increasingly important: what happens in the first six months of employment. 🙌🏼

A situation I have seen more than once:

“We need to dismiss them.”

Okay. What happened?

“Well… they’ve been struggling for a while.”

How long is “a while”?

“About four months.”

Excellent. And what feedback have they had?

“Not much.”

Right.

And what was discussed at probation?

“Nothing formal.”

At this point, HR is expected to perform an employment law exorcism and fix six months of poor management in one meeting.

The better approach starts much earlier.

Before the employee starts:
→ Is the role and expectation clear?

During onboarding:
→ Are they actually being set up to succeed?

At probation:
→ Is there an honest assessment of performance and fit?

When concerns arise:
→ Are they being addressed early, clearly and consistently?

That is where my experience across Talent Acquisition and HR has been particularly valuable.

The recruitment decision is only the beginning. If the process from “we want to hire them” to “we need to dismiss them” is disconnected, the problem is usually not created at the end.

It has been quietly accumulating for months.

The upcoming changes make getting that process right even more important.

And, ideally, mean fewer meetings beginning with: “We need to get rid of them” and ending with everyone looking at HR as though we have a magic wand. (Newsflash, we don’t) 👀

By Lisa Matomola

A key part of our consulting work at Hito HR involves helping organisations attract and hire the right people.

While recruitment may appear straightforward, the reality is often far more complex, particularly for organisations operating within tight budgets.

One lesson has become increasingly clear over the years: Talent is not cheap. Neither is hiring the wrong person.

Whenever I hear concerns about salary expectations, I encourage employers to pause and look beyond the number on the offer letter. Instead of asking, "Can we afford this candidate?" I ask a different question: "Can you afford not to hire them?"

That question often changes the entire conversation.

A few thousand dollars may seem like a significant amount during salary negotiations, but what will it cost if the position remains vacant for another six months? What will it cost if critical projects are delayed because no one has the expertise to lead them?
